total_activity_released_this_phase_EBq: ~0.5_to_1.5 (estimate: all phases total ~12 EBq including noble gases)
dominant_mechanism: Prompt criticality steam explosion (possibly 2 explosions); dispersal of fuel particles graphite and core material; primarily noble gases and volatiles; steam-driven deaerosolization
notes: Noble gas (Xe-133 Kr-85) primary component of initial explosion release; released essentially instantaneously; I-131 volatile released partly as elemental I2 and organic iodides; Cs-137 as CsI and CsOH aerosols; Pu and actinides as fuel particle aerosols; graphite lofted up to 1 km altitude
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D Table D5-D6; OECD-NEA Chernobyl 1996; Sich 1994; 01_source_term_REAL.csv

dominant_mechanism: Graphite fire in reactor core burning at ~1000-1200°C; helicopter sand/boron/lead drops (5100 tonnes deposited) partially reduce fire; radionuclide release driven by combustion aerosols and thermal convection from graphite fire
notes: Daily release declining during this phase; helicopter drops reduced fire but did not extinguish it; sand and dolomite drops briefly suppressed release; boron-10 intended to absorb neutrons (though criticality already ended); 5100 tonnes total drops estimated to have reduced April 28-30 releases
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; OECD-NEA 1996 Radiological Consequences; Sich 1994

dominant_mechanism: Helicopter drops reduced immediate combustion; fuel temperature temporarily lowered; sand/lead partially covering reactor opening reduced aerosol generation; lowest release rate of the entire event
notes: Sand and lead cover created temporary minimum; however reactor core heating continued from radioactive decay heat and possibly residual criticality in graphite-moderated fuel remnants; minimum release approximately 3-4x lower than peak days
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D Figure D-III; OECD-NEA 1996

dominant_mechanism: Core temperature rose to ~1650°C by May 6-7 (higher than initial fire); thermal emission of refractory radionuclides increased dramatically; second spike in atmospheric release; some sources suggest 'thermonuclear heating' hypothesis
notes: May 6-8 is second major release period; long-range contamination of Scandinavian countries partly from this phase; elevated Sr-90 release relative to earlier phases because higher temperature volatilizes more refractory isotopes; OECD-NEA Table II.3 shows May 7 peak in daily emission
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; OECD-NEA 1996 Table II.3; Devell et al. 1986 Nature; 01_source_term_REAL.csv

dominant_mechanism: Graphite fire extinguished May 9-10 by combination of nitrogen injection into reactor space and natural sand/lead thermal insulation; core cooled; aerosol generation ended
notes: Nitrogen injection forced through existing piping removed oxygen; fire extinguished; release rate dropped sharply after May 9; residual releases from contaminated soil and fuel particles continued at very low level for months thereafter; graphite fire extinguishment confirmed by temperature monitoring

dominant_mechanism: Diffuse release from: heated sarcophagus interior; contaminated soil resuspension; rain washing; fuel particle dissolution; no active fire; total residual releases in weeks after fire estimated <5% of total for most isotopes
notes: Post-fire residual releases important for Sr-90 and Pu because their primary release came as fuel particles rather than volatile gases; fuel particles dissolve slowly (years to decades); groundwater transport of Sr-90 from fuel particles continues to present (2026); see fuel_particle_contamination_REAL.csv

UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D Table D6: Cs-137 total atmospheric release 85 PBq ± 30 PBq (range 45-135 PBq); represents ~1.4% of total Cs-137 inventory in Unit 4 core at time of accident (~6000 PBq); see 01_source_term_REAL.csv for full 20-isotope inventory

UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D: I-131 total release 1760 PBq ± 500 PBq; ~55% of total I-131 in core at accident; highly volatile; peak air concentrations drove thyroid dose to children; by October 1986 (10 half-lives) essentially fully decayed

UNSCEAR 2008: Sr-90 total release 10 PBq ± 4 PBq; only ~4% of Sr-90 core inventory; relatively refractory; majority released as fuel particles in near-field; dissolved fraction transported by water (Dnieper system); long-lived (t1/2=28.8yr) ongoing concern

Noble gases (primarily Xe-133 ~6500 PBq; Kr-85 ~33 PBq) released essentially completely and rapidly; no deposition; followed long-range atmospheric transport; Xe-133 detected globally; used as source term fingerprint for accident timing and magnitude; Forsmark Sweden detected Cs-137 on April 28 with Xe-133 simultaneously

Cs-134 total release ~180 PBq (UNSCEAR 2008); Cs-134/Cs-137 activity ratio at release = ~0.57 (Cs-134 t1/2=2.06yr; both are fission products + activation products in proportional amounts at burnup ~10-11 GWd/tU); this ratio is the definitive temporal fingerprint of Chernobyl-origin contamination; see radioactive_decay_chains_REAL.csv

Te-132 (t1/2=3.20 days) total release ~1150 PBq; tellurium volatile at reactor temperatures; significant short-term dose contributor via daughter I-132 (t1/2=2.3h); Te-132 + I-132 important for early dose assessment in first 2-3 weeks; fully decayed within ~2 months

Pu-239+240 total release ~0.013 PBq = 13 TBq (UNSCEAR 2008); << 0.01% of core inventory; refractory oxides deposited within 30-60 km of reactor as hot particles; long-lived (Pu-239 t1/2=24110yr); permanent contamination of near-field; see fuel_particle_contamination_REAL.csv and contamination_zones_REAL.csv

Near-field (<60 km): dominated by fuel particles (hot particles); contains Pu Am Zr Nb Ru Ce; deposited as physical particles settling by gravity; high Sr-90/Cs-137 ratios because Sr relatively refractory. Far-field (>60 km): dominated by volatile aerosols and condensed particulate; primarily Cs-137 Cs-134 I-131; lower Sr-90/Cs-137 ratios; airborne dust sizes 0.5-3 µm settling slowly. This is key for understanding why near-field contamination pattern differs fundamentally from far-field
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; fuel_particle_contamination_REAL.csv; OECD-NEA 1996; Salbu 2001 PMID:11202686

Cs137_fraction_of_isotope_total_released: Initial explosion lofted radioactive material to 1000-1500 m altitude; graphite fragments and corium particles to lower heights (100-500 m); volatile radionuclides (noble gases Cs I) to upper plume; tall initial plume enabled long-range atmospheric transport to Scandinavia in ~36 hours
I131_fraction_of_isotope_total_released: Higher loft height means longer atmospheric residence time and wider geographic spread; HYSPLIT trajectory models and monitoring station data used to reconstruct trajectory; see atmospheric_transport_plume_REAL.csv

Cs137_fraction_of_isotope_total_released: 5100 tonnes of materials dropped on reactor by helicopter: sand (2400t to smother fire); lead (2400t - also for radiation shielding but evidence of effectiveness debated); dolomite (800t to release CO2); clay; boron carbide (neutron absorber). Drops continued until fire extinguished May 9
I131_fraction_of_isotope_total_released: Lead drops were controversial: at high temperature lead may have increased some releases by evaporating; effectiveness of boron uncertain as fission had ceased; sand and dolomite more effective; total 1800+ helicopter sorties; pilots received significant doses; 3 pilots died in helicopter crash Apr 26 (not from radiation)
